opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the way to understand it is that the frontier labs have mostly exhausted the easy part of the open web. The broad, general knowledge that's freely crawlable has largely been absorbed into pre-training. So the marginal gains now come from data that's either hard to get, hard to produce, or simply doesn't exist on the public internet yet.

There are a few buckets. One is proprietary or licensed content: things behind paywalls, archives, specialized corpora, where the owner has leverage and the labs would rather have a clean legal footing than fight over it. Another, which I think is the bigger one, is data that captures expertise and process rather than just facts. If you want a model that can reason like a good lawyer or debug like a senior engineer, you need examples of that work being done, the intermediate steps, the judgment calls, the corrections. That mostly lives in people's heads, so you pay experts to generate it, or to grade and critique model outputs for reinforcement learning.

And then there's a shift from static data to environments and feedback. With agents, it's less about having a big pile of text and more about having tasks, tools, and signals that tell the model whether it actually did the job well. That's expensive to build, and it's a real competitive advantage, so it makes sense to spend on it.

From where I sit, working on how AIs use the web, the interesting part is that it goes both ways. Models pay for data to get better at training time, but increasingly they also need fresh, high-quality information at inference time, when an agent is actually doing research or completing a task. The web was built for humans clicking through pages, not machines trying to get the right answer efficiently. So I think we'll see the economics of data move from one-time training deals toward something more continuous, where the value of good information is priced in every time an AI uses it. That's healthier for the people creating content, too, because it ties their compensation to ongoing usefulness rather than a single bulk sale.

r001.rationale: The response says models increasingly need fresh, high-quality information at inference time and describes ongoing payment for information each time an AI uses it.

r002.rationale: It mentions seeking a clean legal footing for proprietary content, but does not identify protection from liability for training that has already occurred.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that for a long time, the story of model progress was mostly a story about compute and architecture. You scaled up, you got better. But the thing that's become really clear over the last couple of years is that the marginal returns from just scraping more of the open web have gone way down. Most of what's freely available has already been consumed, and a lot of it is low quality, redundant, or increasingly generated by models themselves.

So when a model company pays for data, they're really paying for three things.

The first is scarcity. There's information that just doesn't exist on the public internet. Expert reasoning, the way a tax attorney actually works through an edge case, how an experienced engineer debugs a distributed system, what a doctor is thinking in the moments before they order a test. That tacit knowledge was never written down anywhere. If you want a model to do it, someone has to produce it, and that costs money.

The second is specificity. The frontier is no longer "can the model write a coherent paragraph." It's "can the model do this exact task at the level of a professional." That means you need data that targets the model's actual weaknesses, which requires knowing where it fails and then going out and getting examples that fix it. That's a very different thing from bulk crawling.

And the third, honestly, is legitimacy. Companies want data they can actually use without legal exposure, with clear provenance, where the people who created it were compensated and consented. That's not a nice-to-have anymore.

The frame I find useful is that data has become a form of capital expenditure, in the same way GPUs are. You're not buying a commodity. You're buying capability that you couldn't otherwise get, and the quality of what you buy shows up directly in what the model can do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scarce and targeted data for improving model capabilities, but does not identify fresh data used during inference as a reason to pay.

r002.rationale: It mentions clear provenance and avoiding legal exposure, but does not connect payment to liability protection for training that has already been performed.

astra-6.text:
I think model companies pay for data because they expect it to improve their models. But the value isn’t simply in having more data. It’s in having data that adds something they’re missing—knowledge, examples of a particular task, or feedback that helps distinguish a good answer from a bad one.

So the question becomes: does this data produce a meaningful improvement over what we already have? If it does, and that improvement matters to users, there’s a reason to pay for it. The hard part is figuring out that value before you’ve actually trained on the data.

r001.rationale: The response discusses data improving models and user-facing value, but does not identify access to fresh data during inference as a reason to pay.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention liability protection or covering training that has already been performed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think model companies pay for data because the right data can improve what their models are able to do. But the value isn’t simply in having more of it. It’s in having data that’s relevant, reliable, and gives you something you don’t already have.

So the question is: what capability are you trying to improve, and what data would help you improve it? That could be examples for training, expert feedback, or data that lets you measure whether the model is actually getting better. You’re ultimately paying for the improvement that data makes possible.
